claims.text: Rapid laser ablation produces initially homogeneous, single-solid-solution Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Heating differentiates the elemental mobilities within Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Cu preferentially segregates toward the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Preferential surface segregation produces a disordered, liquid-like interfacial layer before complete melting.
The liquid-like surface layer nucleates complete melting of the nanoparticle.
High configurational entropy in the nanoparticle core delays complete elemental segregation.
Rapid cooling can retain a homogeneous multielement solid solution and suppress segregation or phase separation.
Differences in constituent melting points and surface-energy characteristics govern elemental mobility during heating.
Elements having lower melting points and higher surface energies preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
On rapid cooling, the segregated liquid-like surface layer consolidates back into a homogeneous solid solution.
Single-metal and binary nanoparticles lack the marked elemental-mobility differentiation proposed for the HEA nanoparticles.
Single-metal and binary nanoparticles do not form a similarly graded premelting regime.
Relative to single-metal or binary baselines, the HEA nanoparticles will form a liquid-like surface layer at a lower temperature before bulk melting.
Premelting will produce measurable nanoscale surface-composition gradients in the HEA nanoparticles.
Slower cooling will permit more segregation than rapid quenching.
The proposed mechanism applies to initially homogeneous HEA nanoparticles whose constituents differ significantly in melting temperature and surface energy.
The premelting-to-melting regime for these nanoparticles extends from room temperature to approximately 1200 °C under inert atmosphere.

contradictions.description: The particles are called “heterogeneous” in the hypothesis but are described as initially homogeneous single-phase solid solutions in the initial-state field. This is contradictory unless “heterogeneous” was intended only to mean multielement.
